mainTopic: The story of אונקלוס the convert, אנטונינוס and רבי, and the burning done at the death of kings
overview: This amud opens with a short line that closes the previous story: 'the bundle is separated.' Next comes the story of אונקלוס, a Roman who became a גר. The קיסר sends three troops of soldiers to bring him back, and אונקלוס wins each troop over. He uses פסוקים, then a parable about torches, then the meaning of the מזוזה, until the קיסר gives up. The גמרא then returns to אנטונינוס, using a דרשה to read 'two nations' in רבקה's womb as two great men, אנטונינוס and רבי, and settles a question about whether cucumbers are healthy. Back in the משנה, the גמרא first infers that רבי מאיר and the רבנן disagree about whether burning at a king's death is an idolatrous custom. A ברייתא shows that Jews burn items for kings, so the גמרא explains the argument differently. Everyone agrees burning is a sign of honor, and the only question is which deaths the idolaters celebrate. Finally, the גמרא studies that ברייתא: what may be burned or destroyed for kings and נשיאים, אונקלוס's burning for רבן גמליאל, and cutting animals' hooves. That last discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The bundle is separated
steps.stepSummary: A short closing line that ends the previous story.
steps.simpleTranslation: The bundle has come apart.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the story it was telling before this point with a short, sad saying: 'the bundle is separated.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: A 'bundle' is a picture of a close bond between people. Saying it has come apart means that bond has ended. This line closes the previous story, so the next line starts a brand-new one.

keyTerms.meaning: has come apart, has been separated
a bundle; a picture of a close bond

steps.confusionAlert: This line belongs to the story before it, not to the אונקלוס story that follows. Don't try to connect it to אונקלוס.

phrases.english: The bundle has come apart.
phrases.notes: This is the closing line of the story the גמרא was just telling. A close bond has now ended.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the story from the previous section
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The previous story ends with the image of a close bond that has now come apart.

steps.title: אונקלוס converts and wins over the first troop
steps.stepSummary: אונקלוס converts. The קיסר sends soldiers after him, and אונקלוס draws them in with verses until they convert too.
steps.simpleTranslation: אונקלוס son of קלונימוס converted. The emperor sent a troop of Roman soldiers after him. He drew them in with verses, and they converted.
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. אונקלוס, a Roman, becomes a גר. The emperor sends soldiers to bring him back, but he teaches them פסוקים and they become גרים as well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The soldiers came to arrest אונקלוס, but they ended up joining him. His tool was the words of תורה. This sets the pattern for the rest of the story, where every troop sent against him gets won over.

keyTerms.meaning: he drew them in, attracted them

phrases.english: Onkelos son of Kelonimos converted;
the emperor sent a troop of Romans after him;
he drew them in with verses, and they converted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new story after the previous one closed
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אונקלוס converts and draws the first troop of soldiers to convert through פסוקים.

steps.title: A second troop is sent with orders not to speak
steps.stepSummary: The קיסר sends another troop and tells them not to say anything to אונקלוס.
steps.simpleTranslation: He then sent another troop of Romans after him and told them: Don't say anything at all to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor tries again. This time he warns the soldiers not to talk with אונקלוס at all. This sets up the next move in the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The emperor learned from the first failure. If teaching פסוקים won the soldiers over, then he will cut off conversation completely. The story is building suspense: how will אונקלוס reach them now?

phrases.english: He then sent [another] troop of Romans after him;
phrases.notes: Some versions don't have the word in square brackets. The corrected wording adds it.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: לָא תֵּימְרוּ לֵיהּ וְלָא מִידֵּי.
phrases.english: he said to them: Do not say anything at all to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲדַר שַׁדַּר גּוּנְדָּא דְּרוֹמָאֵי אַחֲרִינָא אַבָּתְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The emperor reacts to the failure of the first troop
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The second troop is ordered not to speak with אונקלוס.

steps.title: The parable of who carries the torch
steps.stepSummary: אונקלוס describes how lower officials carry torches for higher ones, then asks whether the highest ruler carries a torch for ordinary people. They answer no.
steps.simpleTranslation: As they were taking him along, he said to them: Let me just tell you a simple thing. A minor official holds a torch in front of a higher official. The higher official holds it for a duke, the duke for the governor, and the governor for the ruler. Does the ruler hold a torch in front of ordinary people? They said to him: No.
steps.whatsHappening: אונקלוס finds a way around the 'no talking' order. He does not argue about religion. He just asks a simple question about Roman ranks, and the soldiers answer 'no.' This prepares his main point in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Rome, the lower-ranking person carries the light for the higher-ranking one. So the most important person never carries a torch for the people below him. By getting the soldiers to agree to this, אונקלוס sets them up for a surprise.

keyTerms.meaning: just a simple matter, nothing serious

phrases.english: When they were taking him along,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ אֵימָא לְכוּ מִילְּתָא בְּעָלְמָא:
phrases.english: he said to them: Let me tell you just a simple thing:
A minor official holds a torch before a higher official,
the higher official for a duke, the duke for the governor,
the governor for the ruler.

phrases.aramaic: קוֹמָא מִי נָקֵט נוּרָא מִקַּמֵּי אִינָשֵׁי?
phrases.english: Does the ruler hold a torch before ordinary people?
They said to him: No.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: אונקלוס gets around the order not to talk
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the highest ruler ever carries a torch for ordinary people

steps.title: God carries the torch for Israel
steps.stepSummary: אונקלוס points out that הקדוש ברוך הוא Himself lights the way for ישראל, as the פסוק says. The whole troop converts.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: But הקדוש ברוך הוא holds a torch before ישראל, as it is written: 'And ה׳ went before them by day...' They all converted.
steps.whatsHappening: אונקלוס delivers his main point. No human ruler carries a light for his people, but הקדוש ברוך הוא did exactly that for ישראל in the מדבר. The second troop is moved, and they all become גרים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The parable from the step before sets up a contrast. The greatest King of all serves His people personally, which shows how precious ישראל are to Him. The פסוק about the pillar of cloud and fire is the proof.

keyTerms.meaning: the Holy One, Blessed be He

steps.whatToRemember: No human king carries a light for his subjects, but הקדוש ברוך הוא lit the way for ישראל Himself. That showed the soldiers how beloved ישראל are.

phrases.english: He said to them: Yet the Holy One, Blessed be He,
holds a torch before Israel,
as it is written: “And the Lord went before them by day, etc.”
phrases.notes: שמות 13:21. The פסוק goes on to describe the pillar of fire that gave them light at night.

phrases.english: They all converted.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נְקַט נוּרָא קַמֵּי יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the soldiers' 'no' to draw the contrast
steps.raayaObject: That הקדוש ברוך הוא personally serves ישראל, unlike any human ruler

steps.title: A third troop is sent with orders not to talk at all
steps.stepSummary: The קיסר sends yet another troop, now forbidding any conversation with אונקלוס.
steps.simpleTranslation: He then sent another troop after him and told them: Don't have any conversation with him at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor tries a third time, with an even stricter order: no conversation of any kind. This sets up the next scene.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first order was 'don't say anything to him,' and אונקלוס still got the soldiers talking. Now the order is complete silence. The story keeps raising the challenge to show how אונקלוס will still succeed.

phrases.english: He then sent another troop after him;

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: לָא תִּשְׁתַּעוּ מִידֵּי בַּהֲדֵיהּ.
phrases.english: he said to them: Do not converse with him at all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The emperor reacts to the failure of the second troop
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The third troop is forbidden from talking with אונקלוס at all.

steps.title: אונקלוס points to a מזוזה
steps.stepSummary: While being led away, אונקלוס puts his hand on a מזוזה and asks what it is. The soldiers ask him to tell them.
steps.simpleTranslation: As they were holding him and walking, he saw a מזוזה placed on a doorway. He put his hand on it and said to them: What is this? They said to him: You tell us.
steps.whatsHappening: Even with the silence order, אונקלוס sparks curiosity by touching a מזוזה and asking about it. The soldiers themselves invite him to explain, which sets up his answer in the next part of the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אונקלוס doesn't break their rule by preaching. He asks a question, and they choose to start the conversation by saying 'you tell us.' He explains the מזוזה in the next step.

phrases.english: While they were holding him and walking,
he saw a mezuzah that was placed on a doorway.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹתֵיב יְדֵיהּ עֲלַהּ, וַאֲמַר לְהוּ: מַאי הַאי?
phrases.english: He put his hand on it and said to them: What is this?
They said to him: You tell us.

steps.triggerLanguage: אוֹתֵיב יְדֵיהּ עֲלַהּ וַאֲמַר לְהוּ מַאי הַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: אונקלוס finds a way to start a conversation despite the strict silence order
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the מזוזה on the doorway is
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The soldiers ask אונקלוס to explain it. He answers in the next step (Step 8): ה׳ guards His people from outside their homes.

steps.title: אונקלוס explains the מזוזה
steps.stepSummary: אונקלוס explains that a human king sits inside while his servants guard him outside. With הקדוש ברוך הוא it is the reverse: His servants sit inside and He guards them from outside, as the פסוק says.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Normally a human king sits inside and his servants guard him from outside. But הקדוש ברוך הוא is different: His servants are inside, and He guards them from outside, as it says, 'ה׳ will guard your going out and your coming in, from now and forever.'
steps.whatsHappening: אונקלוס answers his own question from Step 7. He tells the soldiers what the מזוזה means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same kind of argument as the torch story, but with a new image. Among people, the lower ones guard the higher one. With ה׳, He Himself guards His people. The מזוזה on the doorway shows ה׳ standing guard outside the Jewish home.

keyTerms.meaning: The normal way of the world
A human king (literally, a king of flesh and blood)

phrases.english: He said to them: The normal way of the world is,
a human king sits inside,
and his servants guard him from outside;
but the Holy One, Blessed be He,
His servants are inside and He guards them from outside,
phrases.notes: His 'servants' are the Jewish people sitting in their homes, with the מזוזה on the doorway outside.

phrases.english: as it says: 'ה׳ will guard your going out and your coming in'
'from now and forever.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the מזוזה that אונקלוס asked in Step 7
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the object on the doorway (the מזוזה)?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It shows that ה׳ guards His people from outside their homes. This is the opposite of a human king, who is guarded by his servants.

steps.title: The soldiers convert and the emperor gives up
steps.stepSummary: This troop also converts. After that, the קיסר stops sending soldiers after אונקלוס.
steps.simpleTranslation: They converted. He did not send anyone after him again.
steps.whatsHappening: The story of אונקלוס ends here. The third troop converts, and the קיסר gives up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All three tries ended the same way, even after the קיסר forbade any conversation. אונקלוס won them over with a single gesture at the מזוזה. Stopping the chase shows that the קיסר admitted defeat.
steps.whatToRemember: Three troops were sent and all three converted. Each time, אונקלוס showed how ה׳'s closeness to ישראל is greater than any human king's relationship with his people.

phrases.english: They converted. He did not send after him anymore.
phrases.notes: The 'he' who stopped sending is the קיסר.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the result of the explanation in Step 8 and closes the story
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The קיסר's attempts failed completely, and אונקלוס was left alone.

steps.title: Two great ones in רבקה's womb: אנטונינוס and רבי
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, quoting רב, reads 'גוים' as 'גיים' (great ones). He says this refers to אנטונינוס and רבי, whose tables never lacked lettuce, cucumber or radish in any season.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And ה׳ said to her: Two nations are in your womb.' רב יהודה said in the name of רב: Don't read it 'גוים' (nations), but 'גיים' (great ones). This means אנטונינוס and רבי. Their tables never lacked lettuce, cucumber or radish, not in summer and not in the rainy season.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to talking about אנטונינוס. It brings a דרשה on a פסוק about רבקה's twins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By changing the reading of one word, the פסוק becomes a prediction about two great people: one from עשו (אנטונינוס) and one from יעקב (רבי). Their greatness shows in their wealth: they had vegetables on the table even when those vegetables were out of season.

keyTerms.meaning: Don't read it as (a way of drawing a lesson by reading a word differently)

steps.confusionAlert: 'אל תקרי' does not mean the פסוק is changed or misspelled. It is a way of drawing an extra lesson from the words while the written text stays the same.

phrases.english: 'And ה׳ said to her: Two nations are in your womb.'
phrases.notes: בראשית 25:23. ה׳ is speaking to רבקה, who was pregnant with יעקב and עשו.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav:
Don't read 'goyim' (nations) but 'geyim' (great ones),
this means Antoninus and Rabbi,
from whose table there never ran out

phrases.aramaic: לֹא חֲזֶרֶת וְלֹא קִישּׁוּת וְלֹא צְנוֹן,
phrases.english: not lettuce, not cucumber, and not radish,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא בִּימוֹת הַחַמָּה וְלֹא בִּימוֹת הַגְּשָׁמִים,
phrases.english: neither in the summer nor in the rainy season,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: אַל תִּקְרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the אונקלוס story and goes back to the topic of אנטונינוס
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'two nations' in רבקה's womb are two great people, אנטונינוס and רבי, who were rich enough to have these vegetables all year round.

steps.title: Why those three vegetables
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why they kept these vegetables: each one is good for digestion.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the Master said: Radish breaks up food, lettuce churns food, and cucumber widens the intestines.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason these three vegetables were always on the table.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These were not just luxuries. Each one has a health benefit for digesting food. This sets up the challenge in the next step, which is about cucumbers.

phrases.english: As the Master said:
radish breaks up food,
lettuce churns food,
cucumber widens the intestines.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason behind the detail about the vegetables in Step 10
steps.raayaObject: Why these three vegetables were always on the table
steps.raayaSupportSource: A known teaching ('דאמר מר') about the health benefits of each vegetable

steps.title: But cucumbers are harmful
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea that cucumbers are healthy. A teaching from the school of רבי ישמעאל says they are as harmful to the body as swords.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the school of רבי ישמעאל taught: Why are they called 'kishu'in'? Because they are as harsh ('kashin') on a person's body as swords!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a contradiction. One teaching says cucumbers are good for you, and another says they are harmful.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The attack is on Step 11's claim that cucumbers widen the intestines. A ברייתא draws the name 'קישואין' from the word 'קשין' (harsh), showing that cucumbers hurt the body. So why would great men eat them every day?

keyTerms.meaning: But wasn't it taught? (introduces a challenge from a ברייתא)
Of the school of רבי ישמעאל

phrases.english: But the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
Why are they called 'kishu'in' (cucumbers)?

phrases.aramaic: מִפְּנֵי שֶׁקָּשִׁין לְגוּפוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם כַּחֲרָבוֹת!
phrases.english: Because they are as harsh to a person's body as swords!
phrases.notes: A play on words: 'kishu'in' sounds like 'kashin', which means harsh.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the health claim about cucumbers in Step 11
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that cucumbers are healthy ('קישות מרחיב מעיים')
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא says cucumbers are harmful like swords, which contradicts the claim that they are good for you.

steps.title: Large versus small cucumbers
steps.stepSummary: There is no contradiction. Large cucumbers are harmful, and small ones are healthy.
steps.simpleTranslation: It's not a problem: this teaching is about big ones, and that teaching is about small ones.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by saying the two teachings are about different sizes of cucumber.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both teachings are true, but each covers a different case. The harmful ones are the large cucumbers. The healthy ones that אנטונינוס and רבי ate are the small ones.

phrases.english: It is not a problem:
this is about big ones, that is about small ones.
phrases.notes: The 'harmful' teaching is about big cucumbers. The healthy ones on the table were small.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא בְּרַבְרְבֵי, הָא בְּזוּטְרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from Step 12
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (each source refers to a different situation)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources seemed to be talking about all cucumbers, so they contradicted each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Large cucumbers are harmful and small cucumbers are healthy.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: day of birth and day of death
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the words of the משנה, 'the day of birth and the day of death', to start discussing them.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'The day of birth and the day of death.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה and quotes the next phrase. This is a setup line that prepares for the inference in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי מאיר lists the king's day of birth and day of death as festivals of idol worship. The רבנן say only a death that includes burning counts. The גמרא is about to draw a conclusion from this disagreement.

keyTerms.meaning: The day of birth (the king's birthday)
The day of death (of the king)

phrases.english: 'The day of birth and the day of death.'
phrases.notes: These are words from the משנה, from רבי מאיר's list of festivals.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the אגדה and goes back to the wording of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר counts the day of a king's death as a festival of idol worship.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: burning is not an idolatrous custom
steps.stepSummary: Since רבי מאיר makes no distinction between a death with burning and one without, the גמרא infers that he holds the burning itself is not an idolatrous custom.
steps.simpleTranslation: This shows that רבי מאיר holds: it makes no difference whether the death includes burning or does not include burning. Either way, they worship idols on that day. So burning is not an idolatrous custom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a conclusion from רבי מאיר's words in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every king's death is a festival, even without burning, then the idol worship is not caused by the burning. So for רבי מאיר, the burning itself is not a non-Jewish religious practice (חוקה).

keyTerms.meaning: A religious custom of the nations (forbidden as חוקות הגוים)

steps.whyThisMatters: If burning is not a חוקה, then doing it is not copying idolatrous customs. This affects whether such burning is allowed.

phrases.english: This implies that Rabbi Meir holds:

phrases.aramaic: לָא שְׁנָא מִיתָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ שְׂרֵיפָה,
phrases.english: there is no difference between a death that includes burning,

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא שְׁנָא מִיתָה שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ שְׂרֵיפָה —
phrases.english: and a death that does not include burning —
they worship idols on it either way,
evidently, burning is not an idolatrous custom.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from the משנה words quoted in Step 14
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to רבי מאיר, the burning at a king's death is not a חוקה.

steps.title: The רבנן: burning is an idolatrous custom
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers the opposite for the רבנן: they hold that burning is an idolatrous custom.
steps.simpleTranslation: This implies that the רבנן hold: burning is an idolatrous custom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא completes the picture by drawing the opposite conclusion for the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן count only a death that includes burning as a festival. That means the burning is what gives the day its idolatrous character. So for them, the burning is a חוקה.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis (the majority view, arguing with רבי מאיר)

steps.whatToRemember: This first reading says the argument is about whether burning is a חוקה: not for רבי מאיר, yes for the רבנן. Step 18 drops this reading.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two sides. The view that includes more days (רבי מאיר) is the one that says burning is NOT a חוקה.

phrases.english: This implies that the Rabbis hold:
burning is an idolatrous custom.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the matching opposite inference for the רבנן, alongside the one about רבי מאיר in Step 15
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to the רבנן, the burning at a king's death is a חוקה, and that is why only such a death counts as a festival.

steps.title: A ברייתא says Jews burn items for kings, so burning can't be idolatrous
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the idea from step 16 that the רבנן view burning as an idolatrous custom. A ברייתא says Jews burn items at a king's death, and the Torah forbids following idolatrous customs.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a ברייתא teaches: we burn items at the death of kings, and this is not one of the דרכי האמורי. If burning were an idolatrous custom, how could we burn? The תורה says, 'And in their statutes you shall not walk'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge the claim that, according to the רבנן, burning is an idolatrous custom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 16 said the רבנן hold that burning is a חוקה, an idolatrous custom. But Jews themselves burn items for their kings, and the Torah forbids copying idolatrous customs. So burning cannot be a חוקה, and the reading of the רבנן falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it taught in a ברייתא? (opens a challenge from a source)
The ways of the Amorites, meaning forbidden non-Jewish customs
'Do not walk in their statutes', the ban on copying non-Jewish practices

phrases.english: But isn't it taught: We burn items upon the death of kings,
and this is not from the ways of the Amorites,
and if it were an idolatrous custom,
how could we burn?
But isn't it written: 'And in their statutes you shall not walk'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the inference about the רבנן made in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the רבנן hold burning is an idolatrous custom (חוקה).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Jews burn items for their kings, and Jews may not follow idolatrous customs, so burning cannot be a חוקה.

steps.title: Everyone agrees burning is honor; the argument is about when idolaters celebrate
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא re-reads the מחלוקת. All agree burning is a sign of importance, not idolatry. רבי מאיר says idolaters celebrate at any death, while the רבנן say they celebrate only at an important death that includes burning.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, everyone agrees burning is not an idolatrous custom; it is a sign of importance. Here is what they argue about: רבי מאיר holds that whether the death includes burning or not, the idolaters worship their idols on that day. The רבנן hold that a death with burning is important to them, so they worship on it, but a death without burning is not important, so they don't.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops its earlier reading and gives a new explanation of what רבי מאיר and the רבנן are really arguing about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The old reading had them arguing about whether burning is idolatrous. Now everyone agrees burning just shows importance. The argument moves to a question of fact: do idolaters hold idol festivities at every death, or only at an important one?

keyTerms.meaning: This is what they argue about

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the old and new readings. The burning is no longer the issue. The question is only whether idolaters celebrate at a death without burning.
steps.whatToRemember: Burning for kings is a sign of honor, not idolatry, according to everyone. The מחלוקת is about which deaths lead idolaters to celebrate.

phrases.english: Rather, everyone agrees
burning is not an idolatrous custom,
rather, it is a sign of importance,
and here they disagree about this:
Rabbi Meir holds: there is no difference whether it is
a death that includes burning,

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא שְׁנָא מִיתָה שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ שְׂרֵיפָה —
phrases.english: or a death that does not include burning;
they worship idols on it,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבָּנַן סָבְרִי — מִיתָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ שְׂרֵיפָה
phrases.english: and the Rabbis hold: a death that includes burning
is important to them, and they worship on it,
but one that does not include burning
is not important, and they do not worship on it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא שְׂרֵיפָה לָאו חוּקָּה הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17 by redefining the מחלוקת.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading of the dispute (אלא): the earlier inference is replaced.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The רבנן distinguish burning because burning itself is idolatrous.
steps.terutzMaskana: Burning is honor for all; the רבנן only hold that idolaters celebrate at important deaths, meaning ones with burning.

steps.title: The ברייתא itself: burning for kings comes from a פסוק and also applies to נשיאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to study the ברייתא it quoted. Burning for kings is not a forbidden custom, because ירמיהו mentions it, and the same is done for נשיאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The matter itself: we burn items at the death of kings, and it is not considered 'the ways of the Amorites', as it says: 'In peace you shall die, and with the burnings of your fathers the kings...' And just as we burn for kings, we burn for נשיאים.
steps.whatsHappening: With the word גופא, the גמרא goes back to look closely at the ברייתא it just used.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא shows burning for kings is a Jewish practice based on a פסוק in ירמיהו. It then adds a new point: the same honor is given to the נשיאים.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The matter itself': the גמרא returns to study a source it quoted
Burnings done in honor of the dead
The heads of the Jewish leadership, the נשיאים

phrases.english: The matter itself: We burn items upon the death of kings,
and it does not fall under the ways of the Amorites,
as it is said: 'In peace you shall die,
and with the burnings of your fathers the kings, etc.'
And just as we burn upon the kings,
so we burn upon the heads of the Sanhedrin.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ברייתא quoted in step 17 to study it on its own.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Burning for kings is allowed, based on ירמיהו 34:5, and the same applies to נשיאים.

steps.title: What is burned: the king's bed and personal items
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains that the items burned are the king's bed and the things he used.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what do they burn for kings? Their beds and the items they used.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues and defines exactly what is burned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This step limits the burning to the king's own bed and personal belongings. This detail sets up the question in step 22.

keyTerms.meaning: The items and utensils they used

phrases.english: And what do they burn upon the kings?
Their beds and the items they used,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא by defining what is burned.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The items burned are the king's bed and personal belongings.

steps.title: The story of אונקלוס burning a fortune for רבן גמליאל
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא tells that when רבן גמליאל הזקן died, אונקלוס הגר burned seventy Tyrian maneh in his honor.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a story: רבן גמליאל הזקן died, and אונקלוס the convert burned seventy Tyrian maneh in his honor.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a real-life example of burning in honor of a נשיא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן גמליאל was a נשיא, so the story shows the burning for נשיאים in practice. But it seems to describe burning money, which does not fit the 'bed and items' rule. The גמרא will raise this next.

keyTerms.meaning: A Tyrian maneh, a valuable coin weight worth one hundred dinars

phrases.english: And there was an incident when Rabban Gamliel the Elder died,
and Onkelos the convert burned upon him
seventy Tyrian maneh.
phrases.notes: A maneh is one hundred dinars, so this comes to seven thousand dinars, a huge sum.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates burning for a נשיא with a story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אונקלוס burned a great amount in honor of רבן גמליאל הזקן.

steps.title: Didn't you say only beds and personal items are burned?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the story seems to describe burning money, while the ברייתא said only beds and personal items are burned.
steps.simpleTranslation: But you said: what do they burn for them? Their beds and their personal items!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices a clash inside the ברייתא between the rule and the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 limited the burning to beds and personal items. The story in step 21 sounds like אונקלוס burned money. Both cannot be read simply.

keyTerms.meaning: But you said... (points out an internal contradiction)

phrases.english: But you said: What do they burn upon them?
Their beds and the items they used!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the story in step 21 using the rule in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The story that אונקלוס burned seventy Tyrian maneh.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Only beds and personal items are burned, so burning money does not fit the rule.

steps.title: He burned items worth seventy Tyrian maneh
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא corrects the reading: אונקלוס burned items worth seventy Tyrian maneh, not the money itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say instead: he burned items worth seventy Tyrian maneh.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the clash by slightly changing how the story is read.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Adding one letter, ב, turns 'seventy maneh' into 'worth seventy maneh'. Now אונקלוס burned beds and personal items of great value, which fits the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Say instead: introduces a corrected reading

steps.whatToRemember: Only a great person's bed and personal items are burned. אונקלוס burned such items worth a fortune, not money.

phrases.english: Say: items worth seventy Tyrian maneh.
phrases.notes: The extra letter ב changes the meaning: he didn't burn the money, he burned things worth that much.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 22.
steps.terutzMaskana: אונקלוס burned beds and personal items worth seventy Tyrian maneh.

steps.title: Challenge: animals' hooves are also cut for kings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether only personal items are destroyed, since a ברייתא says we cut animals' hooves when kings die.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are other things really not destroyed for a king? But a ברייתא teaches: we cut the hooves of animals when kings die, and this is not forbidden as דרכי האמורי!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא from step 20, which said only the king's bed and personal items are destroyed. Another ברייתא says animals are also crippled in his honor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 limited what is destroyed to the king's own things. Animals are not utensils, yet this ברייתא allows cutting their hooves. So it looks like more than personal items may be destroyed.

keyTerms.meaning: We cut the hooves or tendons of an animal, crippling it
Customs of the Amorites: forbidden non-Jewish practices

steps.confusionAlert: Here עוקרין does not mean 'uprooting' plants. It means cutting an animal's hooves or leg tendons so no one can use it anymore.

phrases.english: And other things are not destroyed?
phrases.notes: He means things other than the king's bed and personal items from step 20.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught: we cut the hooves of animals for kings,
and it is not forbidden as the ways of the Amorites!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the money question was settled in step 23, the גמרא tests the 'only personal items' rule against another ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule (step 20) that only the king's bed and used items are destroyed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Animals are not the king's utensils, yet a ברייתא allows cutting their hooves for kings. So the list must be wider than personal items.

steps.title: רב פפא: it means the horse the king rode
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that the ברייתא means only the horse the king himself rode.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: it means the horse that the king rode on.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the challenge by narrowing the ברייתא about cutting hooves. It is only about the king's own riding horse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The king's riding horse counts as one of his personal things, like his bed. So cutting its hooves fits the rule that only things the king used are destroyed. The rule from step 20 still holds.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
It means the horse he rode on.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: סוּס שֶׁרָכַב עָלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the ברייתא is limited to a specific animal
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to allow crippling any animals for a king.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means only the king's own riding horse, which counts as his personal item.

steps.title: Challenge: hooves of kosher animals are also cut
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether kosher animals' hooves are cut too, quoting a ברייתא about cutting hooves without making the animal a טריפה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And kosher animals are not crippled? But a ברייתא teaches: cutting hooves in a way that makes the animal a טריפה is forbidden, and in a way that does not make it a טריפה is allowed. And what is a cutting that does not make it a טריפה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב פפא with a ברייתא about cutting hooves without making the animal a טריפה. The ברייתא ends with a question, and its answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Whether an animal is a טריפה only matters for a kosher animal, because that is the only kind we might eat. So this ברייתא is talking about kosher animals, which a king does not ride. That goes against רב פפא's answer that only the riding horse is crippled.

keyTerms.meaning: Cutting the hooves or tendons of an animal
An animal with a fatal injury, forbidden to eat even if slaughtered

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא's last line, 'what is a cutting that does not make it a טריפה?', is still part of the quote. It is not the גמרא's own question, and its answer comes in the next lines.

phrases.english: And kosher animals are not crippled?
phrases.notes: A king does not ride a kosher animal, like a cow, so רב פפא's answer would leave it out.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָתַנְיָא: עִיקּוּר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ טְרֵיפָה — אָסוּר,
phrases.english: But isn't it taught: cutting the hooves in a way that makes it a טריפה is forbidden,
and cutting that does not make it a טריפה is permitted,
and what is a cutting that does not make it a טריפה?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's answer from step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's claim that only the king's riding horse is crippled
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא talks about whether the cut makes the animal a טריפה, which only matters for a kosher animal. A king does not ride kosher animals, so it seems they were crippled too, not just his horse.
